dietEvidence.body: The skull and dentition indicate herbivory. No gut contents are known; the plants eaten and the feeding style are inferred from anatomy.

sizeNote: Length and mass are estimates from incomplete material, not measurements of a whole animal.
tagline: An iguanodontian with elongated neural spines along the back. The spines supported a ridge or sail-like structure; the soft tissue is not preserved.
summary: An iguanodontian with elongated neural spines along the back. The spines supported a ridge or sail-like structure; the soft tissue is not preserved.

discovery.body: Named by Taquet, 1976. The record is known from Elrhaz Formation, Gadoufaoua. Several partial skeletons, including a relatively complete skull and postcrania.

fossilEvidence.title: Preserved material
fossilEvidence.body: The holotype and referred material come from the Elrhaz Formation at Gadoufaoua, Niger. The hypodigm includes skull and postcranial material; the soft tissue around the neural spines is not preserved.

fossilEvidence.title: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence
fossilEvidence.body: Elrhaz Formation, Gadoufaoua records the species in the Early Cretaceous. The numeric range used here is ≈125–112 Ma, an occurrence estimate rather than a direct date on every specimen.

anatomy.title: Preserved anatomy
anatomy.body: Elongated neural spines run along the back and tail. The skull is deep and the postcranium is robust; the Venice specimen adds anatomical detail but is not a complete skeleton.

behaviour.body: No direct evidence of social or display behaviour. The elongated neural spines are preserved bone; the silhouette and function of the “sail” are reconstructions, not observations.

reconstruction.body: A licensed life reconstruction is assigned to this record and credited in Sources and credits. The species is known from several partial skeletons, including a relatively complete skull and postcrania. The reconstruction is an artist's interpretation of appearance, not a direct observation from the fossil record; preserved integument, where present, is described in the anatomy section, and the soft-tissue outline is otherwise inferred.

confidenceNote: Taquet (1976) described Ouranosaurus from the Elrhaz Formation of Niger. Elongated neural spines form the structure often called a sail, but the connecting soft tissue is not preserved. The animal’s locomotion and the function of the sail remain debated; no gut contents are known.

primer.lead: Ouranosaurus nigeriensis was a large plant-eating ornithopod from the [Early Cretaceous](/deep-time?period=cretaceous) of Niger. It is instantly recognisable for the long neural spines along its back and tail, which supported a sail-like structure.
paragraphs: The spines are preserved bone, but the soft tissue that connected them is not. The animal’s silhouette is therefore a reconstruction. A second specimen, the Venice specimen, adds postcranial anatomy. Locomotion has been reconstructed as facultatively bipedal or predominantly quadrupedal, and the analyses disagree.
Its plant diet is inferred from the skull and teeth. No gut contents are known, and the function of the “sail” — display, thermoregulation or something else — remains unresolved.
primer.takeaway: A sail-backed plant-eater whose most famous feature is still functionally mysterious.
